topic: Jharkhand HC: a disabled candidate who missed a running test by 3 seconds, with no accommodation, must be appointed - reasonable accommodation is a statutory duty of the State under Sections 2(y) and 20, Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016; rules or notifications cannot override the Act (Juthika Pal v. State of Jharkhand, Jharkhand HC, Justice Deepak Roshan, reported 11 Nov 2026)

slides.title: Missed by **3 seconds** - and still appointed
slides.subtitle: The Jharkhand High Court held that a disabled candidate must get **reasonable accommodation** in a government test. It is the State's duty, not a favour.
slides.cite: **Juthika Pal v. State of Jharkhand** · Jharkhand High Court · Justice Deepak Roshan · reported 11 November 2026

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: A test with **no support**
bullets: A woman with a locomotor disability applied for a Chowkidar post reserved for persons with disabilities.
She cleared the written exam, but in the physical test she had to **run with everyone else**, with no extra time and no other help.
She finished in **10 minutes 3 seconds** against a 10-minute limit, and her name was dropped from the merit list.

slides.label: The law
slides.title: **Reasonable accommodation** is a right
bullets: The **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016** bans discrimination in government jobs and requires reasonable accommodation (**Section 20**).
Reasonable accommodation means suitable changes and support so a disabled person can compete fairly, without an unfair burden on the employer (**Section 2(y)**).
The Court called this a **positive duty of the State** to provide extra support, not an optional kindness.

slides.label: Key point
slides.title: A rule cannot **override** the Act
bullets: The State said no rule allowed relaxing the running-test time. The Court said that is **not an excuse**.
In the Court's words, no notification or rule can go beyond the statutory provision made by Parliament.
She had cleared the written test, missed by just **3 seconds**, and reserved disabled posts were still lying vacant.

slides.label: What it means for you
slides.title: Ask for the support you are **owed**
bullets: If you have a disability, a government recruitment must offer **reasonable accommodation** in its tests, in writing where needed.
A missing rule is not a valid reason to deny it - the **Act itself** gives the right.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.
slides.note: Dhyan rahe: this case is about fair accommodation in the test. It does not scrap physical standards or guarantee a job to every applicant.

caption:
Missed the running test by just 3 seconds - and the High Court said she must still be appointed ♿⚖️

The Jharkhand High Court has held that a candidate with a disability is entitled to reasonable accommodation in a government recruitment test. A woman with a locomotor disability had applied for a Chowkidar post reserved for persons with disabilities. She cleared the written exam, but in the physical test she had to run with other candidates with no extra time or support, and finished in 10 minutes 3 seconds against a 10-minute limit. Her name was then dropped from the merit list.

The Court relied on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. Section 20 bans discrimination in government employment and requires reasonable accommodation, and Section 2(y) defines it as suitable changes and support so a disabled person can compete fairly. The Court called this a positive duty of the State, not a favour, and said no rule or notification can go beyond the Act made by Parliament.

Since she had cleared the written test, missed by only 3 seconds, and reserved disabled posts were still vacant, the Court held she was entitled to appointment. The takeaway: if you have a disability, ask for the accommodation the law gives you - a missing rule is not a valid reason to deny it.

Case: Juthika Pal v. State of Jharkhand
Court: Jharkhand High Court, Justice Deepak Roshan, reported 11 November 2026
